clinicalPearls: A congenitally dilated ureter caused by a narrowed, aperistaltic juxtavesical (distal) segment that impedes urine flow into the bladder, with the obstruction being functional rather than a fixed anatomical stenosis in most cases
Classified within the megaureter spectrum as obstructed, refluxing, both, or neither; the primary obstructive type has obstruction without reflux
Commonly detected on antenatal ultrasound as ureteric dilatation with variable pelvicalyceal dilatation, the ureter being widest just above the bladder
May present later with urinary tract infection, loin pain, or haematuria
The distal aperistaltic segment itself is typically of normal calibre; it is the segment above that is dilated
Many cases, especially with preserved function and modest dilatation, improve spontaneously and are managed expectantly with surveillance and often prophylactic antibiotics

Persistent or progressive obstruction with deteriorating function, breakthrough infection, or symptoms is treated by ureteric reimplantation with tapering or, in selected cases, temporising endoscopic or drainage procedures
reference.pathophysiology: In primary obstructive megaureter the terminal ureteric segment adjacent to the bladder is structurally abnormal, with disorganised smooth muscle and excess collagen that render it aperistaltic and non-compliant. Although this segment is usually of normal or near-normal calibre and not stenotic in the classic sense, it fails to transmit peristaltic waves and effectively obstructs the passage of urine into the bladder. Urine therefore accumulates proximally, producing progressive dilatation of the ureter above the junction and, in more severe cases, pelvicalyceal dilatation and impairment of renal function. There is no reflux, distinguishing it from refluxing megaureter.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior urethral valves with secondary upper-tract dilatation
additionalInvestigations: Renal and bladder ultrasound to characterise ureteric and pelvicalyceal dilatation
MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess drainage and differential function
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to exclude reflux and bladder outlet pathology
Serial ultrasound for surveillance of antenatally detected dilatation
Urinalysis and culture when infection is suspected
MR urography in selected cases to define anatomy
redFlags: Declining differential renal function on serial renography
Febrile urinary tract infection or urosepsis in a dilated obstructed system
Obstruction in a solitary functioning kidney
reference.prognosis: The majority of antenatally detected cases with reasonable function stabilise or resolve spontaneously over the first years of life, and reimplantation for persistent obstruction has good results; long-standing severe obstruction can leave permanent functional loss.
pitfalls: Assuming all megaureters are obstructive when reflux or a non-obstructive non-refluxing pattern may be responsible
Operating early on stable dilatation likely to resolve, rather than observing
Misinterpreting a diuretic renogram in an immature kidney or with a full bladder
Failing to exclude reflux and bladder outlet obstruction before attributing dilatation to the distal ureter
management: Expectant management with active surveillance for antenatally detected cases with preserved differential function and modest dilatation, most of which improve spontaneously
Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, particularly in infancy, to reduce urinary tract infection risk
Serial renal tract ultrasound and diuretic MAG3 renography to monitor dilatation and split renal function
Prompt treatment of febrile urinary tract infection with appropriate antibiotics
Ureteric reimplantation with excision or tapering of the aperistaltic distal segment for persistent obstruction, deteriorating function, breakthrough infection or symptoms
Temporising measures in infants too small for reimplantation, such as JJ stenting, endoscopic balloon dilatation or a cutaneous ureterostomy
Long-term paediatric urology and nephrology follow-up with monitoring of renal function
